title: Problem 7.1
hint: Ask of each choice: did a new substance form? A gas, a temperature change, or bubbles can also come from a change of state or dissolving.

title: Problem 7.2
hint: For each row, ask whether the substance after the change is a new substance or the same substance in a different state. A sign alone (a gas, heat) can mislead.

title: Problem 7.3
hint: Separate the three kinds of numbers: a coefficient counts molecules, a subscript counts atoms in one molecule, and anything over the arrow is a catalyst. Check what (g) means.

title: Problem 7.4
hint: Turn names into formulas first (Chapter 4), remembering that hydrogen gas is diatomic. Then count atoms on each side and add coefficients, never changing subscripts.

title: Problem 7.5
hint: (a) Iron(II) is Fe<sup>2+</sup> and sulfide is S<sup>2−</sup>; combine them. (b) Use conservation of mass, counting only the sulfur that ended up in the product.

title: Problem 7.6
hint: Add the masses before and after. Mass is conserved, so where could the missing mass have gone from an open cup that fizzes?

title: Problem 7.7
hint: Start with O: Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> has 3 and CO<sub>2</sub> has 2, so find the smallest number both divide into. Then balance C and Fe, and use the smallest whole numbers.

title: Problem 7.8
hint: (a) Only O needs work. (b) and (c) Treat sulfate and phosphate as units; balance the metal and the polyatomic ions before H.

title: Problem 7.9
hint: Check two things for each choice: are the formulas real (diatomic elements, correct ion ratios), and does every atom count match on both sides?

title: Problem 7.10
hint: Balance C, then H, then O. If the oxygen total on the right is odd, even the odds: double the fuel and start again. Then add the coefficients.

title: Problem 7.11
hint: Treat nitrate and phosphate as units. Start with the precipitate's 3 Ba and 2 PO<sub>4</sub>, then count how many Na and NO<sub>3</sub> that brings in.

title: Problem 7.12
hint: Check each student for three things: is every formula real (nitrogen gas is diatomic), are the atoms balanced, and are the coefficients the smallest whole numbers?

title: Problem 7.13
hint: Read the equation: how many reactants and products are there, and which product is a gas? Match that to a pattern.

title: Problem 7.14
hint: Count reactants and products and look at what kind they are (element, compound, fuel + O<sub>2</sub>). Match each to A + B, AB, A + BC, AB + CD, or fuel + O<sub>2</sub>.

title: Problem 7.15
hint: Use the three steps: letters, formulas, balance. Write the ion charges first, swap-drop to build each product, and remember that Br<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>, and N<sub>2</sub> are diatomic.

title: Problem 7.16
hint: Incomplete combustion means too little O<sub>2</sub>, so the product is CO. Which choice makes CO and is also balanced?

title: Problem 7.17
hint: (a) Balance C, then H, then O, and remember the fuel already supplies some O. (b) What does too little air do to the carbon products?

title: Problem 7.18
hint: Look for two ionic compounds swapping partners (AB + CD). Classify each of the other choices by its pattern too.

title: Problem 7.19
hint: Use the step-by-step classification: is it ionic? Is it an acid or a base on the green-sheet strong list? If not on the list, it is weak.

title: Problem 7.20
hint: Split each soluble ionic compound into its ions, keeping polyatomic ions whole, and use the subscripts for the counts. Is the last compound ionic at all?

title: Problem 7.21
hint: Build each formula by swap-drop, then check the green sheet: AANA compounds are always soluble, and look for the exceptions in each row.

title: Problem 7.22
hint: Check each against the green sheet. Which cation makes every compound soluble, and which anions have exceptions that include these cations?

title: Problem 7.23
hint: Use the three questions in order: is it ionic? Is it an acid or a base, and is it on the strong list? Neither means nonelectrolyte. Count ions with polyatomic ions kept whole.

title: Problem 7.24
hint: Write each dissolving equation. Keep each polyatomic ion whole and count ions from the subscripts. A molecular compound gives no ions.

title: Problem 7.25
hint: Write the molecular equation, decide which product is insoluble, and cancel the spectators. Check that the solid's formula is neutral.

title: Problem 7.26
hint: (a) Swap partners and check solubility. (b) Split every aqueous strong electrolyte; keep the solid together. (c) Cancel ions that are identical on both sides.

title: Problem 7.27
hint: Swap partners and check each product against the green sheet. Remember mercury(I) is Hg<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup>. No insoluble product, water, or gas means NR.

title: Problem 7.28
hint: Write the swapped products and find the insoluble one. Spectators are the ions that stay dissolved and unchanged on both sides.

title: Problem 7.29
hint: (a) Check the sulfate row of the green sheet: which of the two cations is an exception? (c) Check the fluoride row for both cations.

title: Problem 7.30
hint: (a) Swap partners and treat phosphate as a unit. (b) Multiply each ion count by its coefficient. (c) Cancel spectators and check that the charges add to zero.

title: Problem 7.31
hint: (a) Acid + base → water + salt; each OH needs one HCl. (b) Which species are aqueous strong electrolytes? A solid stays together in the net ionic equation.

title: Problem 7.32
hint: Is HClO<sub>4</sub> on the strong-acid list? Is LiClO<sub>4</sub> soluble? Split the strong electrolytes into ions and cancel the spectators.

title: Problem 7.33
hint: Swap partners. If you get H<sub>2</sub>S or NH<sub>4</sub>OH, check the unstable-products table: what does each really become? Watch the solubility of the calcium product.

title: Problem 7.34
hint: Swapping partners gives calcium acetate and H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>. Use the unstable-products table: what does carbonic acid become?

title: Problem 7.35
hint: Swap partners for each pair. Replace any H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>, or NH<sub>4</sub>OH with what it becomes. No precipitate, water, or gas means NR.

title: Problem 7.36
hint: Swap partners for each pair and look for an unstable product (H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>, NH<sub>4</sub>OH, H<sub>2</sub>S) that gives off a gas.

title: Problem 7.37
hint: Apply the rules in order; when two conflict, the earlier one wins. Assign the known atoms, then find the last one by arithmetic so the sum equals the overall charge.

title: Problem 7.38
hint: Check the rule order: which comes first, the fluorine rule or the oxygen rule? Then make the oxidation numbers add to zero.

title: Problem 7.39
hint: (a) Elements are 0; use O = −2 and arithmetic for the metals. (b) An increase is oxidation, a decrease is reduction. (d) Electrons per atom × number of atoms.

title: Problem 7.40
hint: Assign oxidation numbers and find the element whose number decreases. The oxidizing agent is the reactant that contains it.

title: Problem 7.41
hint: (a) Iron loses electrons (written on the right); silver ions gain them (written on the left). (b) Multiply so the electrons match, then add and cancel.

title: Problem 7.42
hint: Assign oxidation numbers on both sides of each equation. A reaction where no oxidation number changes is not redox.

title: Problem 7.43
hint: (a) Use the rule order: H is +1, so solve for O; an element is 0. (b) Follow each O atom to its product and see if its number goes up or down.

title: Problem 7.44
hint: A metal reacts with acid to release H<sub>2</sub> only if it is above H<sub>2</sub> in the activity series. Find each metal's position.

title: Problem 7.45
hint: Compare the free metal with the metal ion (or H<sub>2</sub>) in the compound: a free metal displaces the ions of any metal below it. Balance any polyatomic ions as units.

title: Problem 7.46
hint: A sacrificial anode must be oxidized more easily than iron. Where must that metal sit in the series compared with Fe?

title: Problem 7.47
hint: (a) Turn each observation into a position: above or below H<sub>2</sub>, Zn, and Pb. (b) Pick a metal ion that sits between the candidates.

title: Problem 7.48
hint: A free metal displaces only the ions of a metal below it (or H<sub>2</sub> from acid if it is above H<sub>2</sub>). Compare each pair.

title: Problem 7.49
hint: (a) Potassium replaces one H in water, and hydrogen leaves as H<sub>2</sub>; balance H last. (b) Where is copper compared with H<sub>2</sub>?

title: Problem 7.50
hint: (a) Use the group number for Sr and the green sheet for carbonate. (b) Swap partners and check the carbonate row. (c) Cancel the spectators.

title: Problem 7.51
hint: (a) Balance C, then H, then O, remembering the fuel supplies one O. (b) Add atomic masses × subscripts. (c) Use conservation of mass in the sealed container.

title: Problem 7.52
hint: (a) Use swap-drop for copper(II) and chloride. (b) Compare tin and copper in the series. (d) Oxidation puts electrons on the right; reduction on the left.

title: Problem 7.53
hint: Write the correct salt formula from the ion charges, then check the unstable-products table: what does H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> become?

title: Problem 7.54
hint: (a) Count the reactants and products. (b) Add atomic masses. (c) Use conservation of mass: the gases are whatever mass left the crucible.

title: Problem 7.55
hint: For each half-reaction: balance atoms other than O and H, then O with H<sub>2</sub>O, H with H<sup>+</sup>, and charge with electrons. Then match the electrons and add.

title: Problem 7.56
hint: Which process, oxidation or reduction, happens at the anode? Track each element's oxidation number from the reactants to LiI.

title: Problem 7.57
hint: Write water as HOH and zig-zag: start with phosphate, zig to its partner H, zag to OH, then zig to Sr.

title: Problem 7.58
hint: Use the three steps: letters, formulas, balance. (a) A halogen replaces the anion. (b) A metal replaces the cation (H<sup>+</sup>). (c) Burns in air means fuel + O<sub>2</sub>.

title: Problem 7.59
hint: Use the step-by-step classification: H in front marks an acid. Is that acid on the green-sheet strong-acid list?

title: Problem 7.60
hint: Follow the full routine: names to formulas, swap-drop, balance (zig-zag), label phases, split the aqueous strong electrolytes, and cancel the spectators.

title: Problem 7.61
hint: Swap partners, then check the unstable-products table for H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>. In the net ionic equation, keep the bisulfite ion whole.

title: Problem 7.62
hint: (a) Do any oxidation numbers change from the elements? (b) Al loses electrons; O<sub>2</sub> gains them. (c) Find the least common multiple. (d) Which rule comes first for Li and H?

title: Problem 7.63
hint: Check both atoms and charge for each choice. How many electrons does Zn lose, and how many does each Ag<sup>+</sup> gain?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Write the two half-reactions. For the nitrate half, balance N, then O with H<sub>2</sub>O, H with H<sup>+</sup>, and charge with electrons. Then match the electrons.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: The anode is where oxidation happens. Which metal is higher in the activity series and so loses electrons?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: For each, ask whether a new substance forms. A change of state or dissolving keeps the same substance.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Turn each name into a formula with a phase label: oxygen gas is diatomic, and Mg<sup>2+</sup> with O<sup>2−</sup> gives the oxide.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Use the law of conservation of mass: in a sealed flask, total mass of products equals total mass of reactants.
why: Mass is conserved in a sealed flask, so the water's mass equals the total mass of hydrogen and oxygen that reacted.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Start with O: 2 in O<sub>2</sub> and 3 in Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. Find the smallest number both divide into, then balance Al last.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Count Cl and H on each side. Balance with a coefficient on HCl, never by changing a subscript.
why: ZnCl<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> each need 2 Cl and 2 H, so a coefficient of 2 on HCl balances both while Zn is already 1 = 1.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Balance C, then H, then O. Count the O on the right after C and H; if it is even, divide by 2 for O<sub>2</sub>.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Write water as HOH. Start with sulfate, zig to its partner H, zag to OH, then zig to K.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Balance C, then H, and count the O on the right. If the total is odd, double the fuel and rebalance.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Count reactants and products: one reactant breaking apart, an element replacing another, or elements joining into one product?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Supply CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. Balance C, then H, then O, remembering the fuel's own O atom.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Two ionic compounds: swap partners (outside–inside), swap-drop the charges, and check the green sheet for the insoluble product.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: A halogen forms an anion, so it replaces the anion. Write the products, then balance with iodine as diatomic.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Letters, formulas, balance: Mg replaces H<sup>+</sup>. Swap-drop Mg<sup>2+</sup> with PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>, then balance phosphate as a unit and leave the lonely Mg for last.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{6}\)
hint: Burns in air means fuel + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O. Balance C, then H, then O.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Ask the three questions: is it ionic? Is it an acid or a base on the strong list? Neither means nonelectrolyte.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Keep the nitrate ion whole; the subscript after the parentheses gives how many nitrate ions form.
why: Aluminum nitrate is a soluble ionic compound, so it separates into one Al<sup>3+</sup> and three NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ions, which keep their own covalent bonds.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Check each against the green sheet: AANA compounds (including Group 1 and ammonium) are always soluble. Look up each anion's row and its exceptions.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Is magnesium nitrate a soluble strong electrolyte? Then check two things: are polyatomic ions kept whole, and is the ion ratio the one in the formula?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Ask the three questions: ionic? Acid (H in front) or base (OH in back) on the strong list? Neither means nonelectrolyte.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Swap partners and find the insoluble product with the green sheet. Write only the ions that build that solid.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Swap partners: check the fluoride row of the green sheet for Sr<sup>2+</sup>. If a solid forms, write only the ions that build it.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Swap partners and swap-drop the charges. Check the hydroxide row for Fe<sup>3+</sup>, then balance with chloride and hydroxide as units.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Names to formulas, swap partners, balance, label phases. Split the aqueous compounds into ions, cancel the spectators, and reduce the coefficients if you can.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: The product marked (s) is the only one not aqueous. Build it from its ions; everything else is a spectator.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Acid + base → water + salt. Match H<sup>+</sup> to OH<sup>−</sup>: Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> has two OH.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Swap partners, then use the unstable-products table: what does H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> become?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Swap partners and check: does a precipitate, water, or a gas form?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Balance with H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> written in, then replace it with what it becomes. Cancel the spectators for the net ionic equation.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Write the complete ionic equation (water and the gas stay whole), cancel the spectators, and reduce the coefficients.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Apply the rules in order: K is +1, H is +1, O is −2. Find the last atom by arithmetic so the sum equals zero.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Assign oxidation numbers before and after: an increase is oxidation, a decrease is reduction. Count electrons per atom × number of atoms.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Oxidation: Mg loses electrons (on the right). Reduction: Ag<sup>+</sup> gains electrons (on the left). Multiply so the electrons match, then add.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Look at which side the electrons are on: lost electrons (on the right) mean oxidation; gained electrons (on the left) mean reduction.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Ca loses electrons; O<sub>2</sub> gains them. Match the electrons, then use the rule order for CaH<sub>2</sub>: the Group 2 rule comes before the hydrogen rule.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{6}\)
hint: Assign oxidation numbers to every element on both sides and look for any change. If nothing changes, no electrons moved.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Is zinc above or below H<sub>2</sub> in the activity series? If above, it displaces hydrogen from the acid.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: A free metal displaces the ions of any metal below it. Which of the two metals is above silver?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Find tin and aluminum in the activity series. Can a free metal displace the ions of a metal above it?
why: A free metal displaces only the ions of a metal below it, and aluminum is above tin, so Sn cannot displace Al<sup>3+</sup>.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Compare the free metal with the metal ion or H<sub>2</sub> in the compound. If the free metal is higher, it reacts; balance chloride and nitrate as units.
